The purpose of this notebook is to allow the NPS team to explore the results
from the sea level rise (SLR) inundation analysis. The data sets were processed
in `rapid_data_processing.Rmd` following the pattern that has been established
for the previous rapid assessment parameters.

The SLR inundation analysis within this notebook concerns itself with exposure.
We are trying to determine what the projected inundation risk of water supplies
of national parks are.

We will start this notebook by pulling in different data sets. We will avoid
generating data here (except for those data manipulations that are necessary for
visualization). Information about where this data was generated will be related
as well.

# Establish environment

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Set up work space
source("setup.R")
```

## Interagency Task Force sea level rise (SLR) projections

These data were sourced from: [Global and Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios for
the United States: Updated Mean Projections and Extreme Water Level
Probabilities Along U.S. Coastlines](https://zenodo.org/records/5951626)

The report that this data come from can be found here: [2022 Technical
Report](https://earth.gov/sealevel/us/resources/2022-sea-level-rise-technical-report/)

An interactive tool displaying these data can be found here: [Interagency Sea
Level Rise Scenario Tool](https://sealevel.nasa.gov/task-force-scenario-tool)

These data were made by the [Interagency Sea Level Task
Force](https://earth.gov/sealevel/us/about/interagency-sea-level-task-force/).
This working group consists of members from NOAA, NASA, JPL, USGS, EPA, FEMA,
DoD, and USACE.

These data are the projections (scenarios) of SLR from the interagency report.

### Read in the SLR projections from ITF

```{r}
slr_projections <- terra::rast(here("data", "all", "coast_comp_data", 
                                    "interagency_report", "generated_products",
                                    "itf_slr_projections_2050_83rd.tif"))
```

### Read in a coastal sample of the inundation projections

This is a subset of the ITF SLR projection data that was generated in 
`rapid_data_processing.Rmd` under:

```

### Generate US Coast subset of ITF SLR projections
```


## Read in the percent change in inundation data

You could find how these data were generated in `src/rapid/calc_inundation_exposure.R`,
whose function was called in `rapid_workflow.Rmd`.

```{r}
# Buffered water supplies with percent change in inundation
ws_inun_pct_delta <- sf::st_read(here("data", "all", "coast_comp_data", 
                                      "NOAA_SLRV_2022", "inundation_data",
                                      "inundation_exposure_(sys.date).csv"))
```

### Join the percent change dataset with the overall buffered water supply dataset

The buffered water supplies with percent change in inundation dataset only has
those data that were relevant to this analysis. That ends up being about 36 park
units and 305 unique water supplies that have a change.

```{r}
# All buffered water supplies with their percent change
buffered_ws <- left_join(ws_inun_proj_reg, ws_inun_pct_delta)
```

# Explore...

Now that we have read in all of the data let's explore the analysis.

The data that we used for this analysis is in two parts. The first is the
projected increase in SLR for a region, and the second is the inundation
surfaces that are related to the projected increase in a region.

## Water supply specific SLR projections

The first thing that we needed to figure out was what the projected increase in
SLR was a for a water supply. We did this by extracting the values from the SLR
projection raster we generated that were related to each water supply.

Here is an example of what it looked like. Note that this raster is not the same
one that was used for the analysis. For the actual analysis we used the entire
projection raster for this extraction, but that is too big for us to visualize
here.

```{r}
# Visualization of the projections with the water supplies
mapview(coast_projections) + mapview(water_supplies)
```

```{r}
# Example of the dataset results
kable(ws_inun_proj) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE) %>%
  kable_paper(full_width = FALSE) 
```

## Water supply specific inundation surfaces

Once we had the SLR projection information for each water supply we needed to
find the right inundation surfaces specific to each water supply.

Here is an example of the way that we determined the region:

```{r}
# Visualization of the water supplies with the CA south region
sample_rast <- terra::rast(here("data", "all", "coast_comp_data",
                                "NOAA_SLRV_2022", "Extent_Rasters",
                                "CA", "CA_South_connectRaster_0_0.tif"))

terra::crs(sample_rast) <-  "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"
sample_rast <- terra::trim(sample_rast)
sample_rast <- terra::ext(sample_rast)
bbox_poly <- terra::as.polygons(sample_rast)
terra::crs(bbox_poly) <- "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"
bbox_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(bbox_poly)
sf::st_crs(bbox_sf) <- 4326
```

```{r}
mapview(bbox_sf, col.regions = "grey", alpha.regions = 0.3) + 
  mapview(water_supplies)
```

```{r}
# Example of the dataset results
kable(ws_inun_proj_reg) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE) %>%
  kable_paper(full_width = FALSE) 
```

## Water supply specific inundation changes

Now that we have the projected SLR changes and the regions that are specific to
each water supply we can assess the inundation risks.

We did this by taking a count of the pixels in the buffer region around the
water supplies which are inundated under 0 feet of inundation, and comparing
that to their projected inundation surfaces

```{r}
hatu_sample <- ws_inun_pct_delta_final %>%
  filter(inundation_region == "MD_East_connectRaster")

# Process HATU rasters with aggregation
hatu_ref_processed <- terra::rast(here("data", "all", "coast_comp_data",
                                      "NOAA_SLRV_2022", "Extent_Rasters",
                                      "MD", "MD_East_connectRaster_0.tif")) %>%
  terra::trim() %>%
  terra::aggregate(fact = 10, fun = "mean")


hatu_proj_processed <- terra::rast(here("data", "all", "coast_comp_data",
                                       "NOAA_SLRV_2022", "Extent_Rasters",
                                       "MD", "MD_East_connectRaster_2_5.tif")) %>%
  terra::trim() %>%
  terra::aggregate(fact = 10, fun = "mean")
```

```{r}
# Create layered mapview
mapview(hatu_proj_processed, 
        col.regions = "steelblue4", 
        alpha.regions = 0.7,
        layer.name = "Projected") +
mapview(hatu_ref_processed, 
        col.regions = "darkgreen", 
        alpha.regions = 0.8,
        layer.name = "Reference") +
mapview(hatu_sample, 
        col.regions = "darkred", 
        alpha.regions = 0.6,
        layer.name = "HATU Water Supplies")

```

# Histograms...

```{r}
library(patchwork)

coast_histogram <- function(data, column_name, dataset_name) {
  # Calculate statistics
  stats <- data %>% 
    summarise(
      n = sum(!is.na(.data[[column_name]])),
      min = min(.data[[column_name]], na.rm = TRUE),
      q1 = quantile(.data[[column_name]], 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
      median = median(.data[[column_name]], na.rm = TRUE), 
      q3 = quantile(.data[[column_name]], 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
      max = max(.data[[column_name]], na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  
  # Format summary for display
  summary_text <- paste0(
    "n = ", scales::comma(stats$n), "\n",
    "Min: ", scales::comma(round(stats$min, 1)), "\n",
    "Q1: ", scales::comma(round(stats$q1, 1)), "\n", 
    "Median: ", scales::comma(round(stats$median, 1)), "\n",
    "Q3: ", scales::comma(round(stats$q3, 1)), "\n",
    "Max: ", scales::comma(round(stats$max, 1))
  )
  
  # Determine if log scale needed (high skew)
  use_log <- (stats$max / stats$median) > 100 && stats$median > 0
  
  p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[column_name]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#2C3E50", alpha = 0.8, color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(stats$median, stats$q1, stats$q3), 
               color = c("#E74C3C", "#F39C12", "#F39C12"), 
               linewidth = c(1.2, 0.8, 0.8),
               linetype = c("solid", "dashed", "dashed")) +
    annotate("text", x = Inf, y = Inf, label = summary_text,
             hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.05, size = 3.5, family = "serif",
             color = "#2C3E50",
             bbox = list(boxstyle = "round,pad=0.4", facecolor = "white", 
                         edgecolor = "#BDC3C7", linewidth = 0.5)) +
    labs(
      title = str_to_title(gsub("_", " ", column_name)),
      subtitle = paste("Dataset:", dataset_name),
      x = NULL, y = "Count"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      text = element_text(family = "serif", color = "#2C3E50"),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5, color = "#7F8C8D"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#ECF0F1", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#ECF0F1", linewidth = 0.3)
    )
  
  # Apply log scale if needed
  if (use_log) {
    p <- p + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma_format())
  } else {
    p <- p + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format())
  }
  
  return(p)
}

# Generate comparison plots for key metrics
key_metrics <- c("ref_coverage_pct", "proj_coverage_pct", "pct_point_change", 
                 "relative_pct_change", "abs_pct_point_change")

# Create paired plots for comparison
comparison_plots <- map(key_metrics, function(metric) {
  p1 <- coast_histogram(ws_inun_pct_delta_final, metric, "Waters with Changes Only")
  p2 <- coast_histogram(buffered_ws, metric, "All Water Supplies")
  
  # Combine with patchwork
  combined <- p1 + p2 + plot_layout(ncol = 2)
  combined <- combined + plot_annotation(
    title = paste("Comparison:", str_to_title(gsub("_", " ", metric))),
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
  )
  return(combined)
})

# Display plots
walk(comparison_plots, print)
```
